Schumann resonance – the Earth's natural "hum": history, links and forecast

Lightning around the world makes the space between the ground and the upper atmosphere ring like a bell at about 7.8 Hz. Three stations record it: Antarctica (Vernadsky), Arctic (Svalbard) and Siberia (Tomsk). "North-south" and "east-west" are the two directions each station's sensor listens in.

All hum values here are digitized estimates, read pixel-by-pixel off published charts: Antarctica (Vernadsky) and Arctic (Svalbard, SOUSY) daily line charts and spectrograms (Zenodo), plus Siberia (Tomsk) charts (Internet Archive snapshots, values read by OCR). Pitch error is about ±0.003–0.01 Hz. Strength is relative (dB at Vernadsky, chart units at Tomsk), not calibrated. Each station measures its own local field, so stations do not track each other day to day.

What the words mean
  • Main Schumann tone, Antarctica (Vernadsky), north-south sensor (Hz) – The Earth–sky cavity hums at about 7.8 Hz, driven by lightning worldwide. This is the pitch of that main hum.
  • Schumann signal strength, Antarctica (Vernadsky), north-south sensor – How loud the main ~7.8 Hz hum is (relative units, not comparable between stations).
  • Geomagnetic storm level (0–9) – How shaken Earth's magnetic field is. 5+ is a storm; 7+ is strong.
  • Magnetic storm depth – How far the magnetic field dips during a storm. More negative = stronger storm.
  • Northern lights activity – Strength of the electric currents that light up the aurora.
  • Sun's radio brightness – Radio glow from the Sun; rises and falls with the 11-year sunspot cycle.
  • Solar wind magnetic direction – Negative (southward) lets solar energy into Earth's field more easily.
  • Solar radiation storm level – Amount of high-energy protons from the Sun (log scale).
  • Link strength (−1 to +1) – 0 = no link; + = rise together; − = one rises as the other falls.
  • Chance it's a fluke (after correction) – Adjusted for running many tests. Under 0.05 = probably real.

Daily links that are probably real (chance of a fluke under 5% after correction), strongest per pair

Each link is measured after removing weekday, month, year and holiday effects, so the slow 11-year sun cycle is taken out here (it is tested separately on monthly data). "Change per typical swing" = how much the hum moves when the cause moves by a normal amount.

Is the forecast really better than guessing? (tested on 2016–2020)

Improvement = how much smaller the forecast's errors are than the best simple guess (0.10 = 10% smaller). "Chance it's a fluke" comes from re-testing on thousands of shuffled 30-day blocks.
